pageCache.text:
‘Fun and caring’ Minerva helps children ‘to become better’, says Ofsted
Children enjoy life at ‘inclusive’ Taunton’s Minerva Primary School, which ‘challenges them to learn’ and gives them ‘the courage to try new things’, according to Ofsted.
In the school’s first inspection under the watchdog’s new framework, Minerva was told it meets expectations in all areas: leadership, teaching and curriculum, inclusion, early years, pupil attendance and behaviour, and wellbeing and achievement.
The school was additionally praised for its effective safeguarding by inspectors who also highlighted its ‘calm and orderly’ atmosphere, and praised the ‘high expectations’ which staff hold for all children.
In his report, lead inspector Ben Jordan wrote: “Pupils enjoy coming to Minerva Primary school. They describe it as a fun and caring place which ‘challenges them to learn’.
“Pupils understand how the school values help them to become better individuals who have the courage to try new things and to work as part of a team
“Current pupils now attend more frequently than those in the past. Pupils have a clear understanding of why attending school is important. Across the school, pupils respond well to the school’s high expectations for their behaviour and conduct.
“Pupils enjoy the opportunities on offer to them. They take pride in their leadership roles such as members of the pupil parliament and librarians. They say that these roles enable them to set a positive example to others and help them to make their school a better place.”
Ofsted’s inspection team went on to praise Minerva in a number of key areas.
On pupil achievement, they said: “Pupils make positive progress from their starting points. This is particularly the case for those who are disadvantaged.
“By the time pupils leave the school, they are increasingly well prepared for the next stage of their education.”
On pupil behaviour, Ofsted said: “Staff understand and consistently follow the school’s behaviour policy, which has positive and respectful relationships at its core.
“The atmosphere in classes and during social times is calm and purposeful. Pupils are polite and well-mannered. They greet visitors with a warm smile. Pupils know that any form of discrimination will not be tolerated.”
On early years provision, inspectors said: “Staff take time to forge positive relationships with children. They work closely with parents and carers to involve them in their child’s learning.
“Children make positive progress through the early years curriculum which prepares them well for Year 1.”
On inclusion, the report said: “Leaders ensure that the additional funding the school receives enables disadvantaged pupils to access everything the school has to offer.
“They rigorously analyse the impact of their actions. Academic and wellbeing barriers disadvantaged pupils face close quickly because of this.”
And on school leadership, Ofsted said: “Leaders, members of the academy council and trustees have an ambitious vision for the school. They know the school and the community it serves well. Since joining the trust, leaders have improved many aspects of the school’s work.
“Pupils, particularly those with SEND and those who are disadvantaged, are at the heart of all decisions that leaders make.”
Ofsted’s findings have been welcomed by leaders at both Minerva and its parent trust the Cabot Learning Federation.
Gareth Nation, Principal at Minerva Primary School, said:
“We are delighted with the findings of this report. It marks a significant milestone in Minerva Primary School’s ongoing improvement and reflects the dedication, ambition and hard work of everyone connected to the school.
“We are particularly thrilled that inspectors recognised the positive progress pupils are making, not only academically, but also as holistic, well-rounded individuals who leave the school well prepared for the next stage of their educational journey. This recognition reflects our commitment to developing confident, capable and resilient young people who are equipped to thrive in an ever-changing world.
“The staff at Minerva Primary School are remarkable individuals whose collective commitment and dedication make the school a truly special place. Their unwavering investment in the children, families and wider community they serve is evident in everything they do. It is both a pleasure and a privilege to work alongside them, and I have the utmost respect for their professionalism, care and determination.
“Minerva Primary is a school where children know they are safe, where they belong and where they know they matter. Pupils receive not only a high standard of education, but also exceptional care, understanding and challenge.
“Together, these experiences help children understand that while life will inevitably bring challenges, they have the confidence, resilience and character to overcome them and flourish. We are incredibly proud of what has been achieved and excited about the next chapter in the school’s continuing journey of excellence.”
Steve Taylor, Chief Executive Officer of the Cabot Learning Federation, said:
“I’m so delighted for the hard-working and expert team at Minerva, and for the community. After almost 20 years, the families once again have a school that they not only love, but that now publicly stacks up against any school in the country in terms of the quality of provision.”

Ofsted Inspection Result
Dear parents and carers
I am delighted to share with you the outcome of our recent Ofsted inspection and the publication of the inspection report.
We are incredibly pleased with the findings, which recognise the significant progress Minerva Primary School has made and reflect the dedication, ambition and hard work of our entire school community.
The report highlights that Minerva Primary School is a place where children feel safe, valued and included. Inspectors recognised the positive progress that pupils make, not only in their academic learning but also in their personal development. We are particularly proud that the report acknowledges how well our pupils are prepared for the next stage of their education and how effectively we support them to become confident, resilient and well-rounded young people.
The inspection team also recognised the strength of our staff and their unwavering commitment to ensuring every child succeeds. Their care, expertise and determination, alongside the support of our families, help create a school where children know they belong and where they are encouraged to aim high and achieve their potential. At Minerva, we believe that education is about more than academic success alone. We want every child to leave us with the knowledge, skills, character and confidence they need to flourish in life. It is therefore particularly pleasing that inspectors recognised the exceptional care, understanding and challenge that pupils receive throughout their time with us.
This outcome is a testament to the collective efforts of our staff, academy councillors, volunteers, pupils, parents and carers. Thank you for the confidence, support and partnership you continue to show the school. Together, we have created a community that enables children to thrive, and we are immensely proud of what has been achieved.
While we will take time to celebrate this important milestone, we remain ambitious for our pupils and committed to building on these successes and improving children’s attendance with your support. We look forward to continuing to work together as we strive for even greater excellence in the years ahead.
The full inspection report will shortly be available to read on Ofsted’s website.
Thank you once again for your continued support.
Gareth Nation Principal

pageCache.text:
Reminder about fidget toys (including squishies)
Dear parents and carers
I would like to take this opportunity to remind you of our approach to the use of fidget toys (including squishies) in school.
Recently, we have seen a significant increase in children bringing a variety of fidget items and toys into school. Whilst these items are often brought with good intentions, we would like to remind families that fidget toys are not toys to be played with during lessons and, in most cases, they do not support learning.
Research and educational experience show that fidget items can often divide a child’s attention rather than improve it. Whilst there are some very specific circumstances where a carefully selected sensory tool may support a child’s engagement, these situations are relatively uncommon and should be considered on an individual basis. More frequently, fidget toys become a distraction to the child using them and to those around them, reducing learning time and concentration.
We are increasingly finding that staff need to ask children to put these items away in their bags during the school day. Unfortunately, this can interrupt learning, lead to unnecessary discussions during lesson time, and can be upsetting for children who have brought the items in expecting to use them.
To ensure consistency across the school and to minimise disruptions to learning, please do not send your child into school with fidget toys or other toys (including squishies) unless you have had a conversation with Mrs Billington and it has been agreed that a specific fidget tool is the most appropriate support for an identified need. In these cases, the item will be carefully matched to the need your child is presenting with and monitored to ensure it is having a positive impact on their engagement and learning.
We greatly appreciate your support in helping us maintain a calm, focused learning environment for all children. If you have any questions or concerns regarding your child’s sensory or attention needs, please do not hesitate to contact Mrs Billington.
Thank you for your continued support.
Mr Gareth Nation Principal

River Tone class staffing update
Dear parents and carers
I am writing to inform you that Ms Crys Poole will be leaving Minerva Primary School on 12 October 2026 to move on to pastures new. We are incredibly grateful for the dedication, care and commitment she has shown throughout her time at MPS. Ms Poole has made a positive contribution to the lives of many children and families and has been a valued member of our staff team. On behalf of the staff, pupils and wider community, I would like to extend our sincere thanks and best wishes for the future.
We recognise that changes in staffing can sometimes be unsettling, particularly for our youngest children in the Early Years Foundation Stage. Ensuring that children feel safe, secure and supported during periods of transition is always a priority for us. As with all transitions at MPS, we will take a carefully planned and child-centred approach to ensure continuity of care, learning and relationships.
To support this process Mrs Selwood, who currently works with the children in River Tone each Friday, will move into the class full-time. This provides an important level of consistency, as Mrs Selwood is already a familiar face to the children and families and she knows the school, routines, expectations and curriculum well.
Over the past week, Ms Poole and Mrs Selwood have been working closely together to ensure a smooth handover of information, routines and individual children’s needs. This will help provide a seamless transition and ensure that children continue to receive the high-quality care and education they deserve.
Looking ahead, the school will be advertising for an EYFS Lead to join our team. We are committed to securing the very best provision for our youngest learners and will keep families informed as the recruitment process progresses.
Thank you for your continued support and understanding. I know you will join me in thanking Ms Poole for her contribution to MPS and wishing her every success and happiness in the next chapter of her career.
Mr Gareth Nation Principal

Building relationships
Our school culture and ethos are inspired by trauma-informed approaches and the supporting science. Through developing a trauma and mental health informed approach, we believe we are supporting the current, and future, positive mental health and resilience of our children and the community we serve, which will enable them to engage fully in life and learning. We strongly believe in the power of relationships, and that all interactions are the opportunity for a positive intervention. We believe all children need to feel safe and emotionally supported in school for any chance of academic success.
We recognise the impact of trauma on brain development and are mindful that children’s responses are due to unavoidable chemical reactions in their brains, rather than ‘negative choices’.
The evidence-based research that underpins all of our SEMH interventions is based on three key models:
Model one – ACES and protective factors
We understand the devastating impact of childhood adversity experiences (ACE) on long-term mental and physical health, but more importantly, we recognise that through ‘protective factors’, we can mitigate the potential impact of early trauma and/or interrupt the progression from early adversity to mental ill-health and early death. Therefore, it is fundamental that wherever possible, we put these key protective factors in place to support all of our vulnerable children’s short and long term mental, physical and societal ill-health.
Protective factors include:
“One trusted emotionally available adult in the school, community or home before the age of 18 can make all the difference. For many children this trusted adult will be someone at school.” (TIS 2019)
Someone in my childhood believed in me.
Model two – The neuroscience of mental health and Panksepp’s emotional system
When planning our interventions and whole school approach to SEMH, we believe having knowledge of the neuroscience of mental ill-health is essential; we place particular importance to the Panksepp emotional system.
Panksepp’s emotional system identifies genetically-ingrained emotion systems in the brain:
RAGE, FEAR, PANIC/GRIEF (trigger stress hormones)
SEEKING and PLAY (trigger pro-social chemicals)
Each system can be overactive, under-active or optimally activated. Children who have suffered trauma tend to have overactive (RAGE, FEAR, PANIC/GRIEF) systems and underactive (CARE, SEEKING and PLAY) systems, resulting in behaviours related to stress, anxiety, depression and anger.
Through our approach and interventions, we hope to activate the pro-social systems of CARE, SEEKING and PLAY in order to restore a balance of the systems, which underpins positive mental health. We do not expect a child who has an overactive RAGE, FEAR or PANIC system to be able to successfully manage the demands of school life without extra purposeful interventions to activate the pro-social systems.
By activating these systems we can:
‘’The ability to form meaningful relationships is fundamental to mental health and happiness. It’s the quality of contact we have with other people that is arguably the most important determining factor in our quality of life. We can only truly develop ourselves through relationships with others.’’ (TISUK 2019)
Our school is invested in supporting the very best possible relational health. Therefore, we are committed to implementing as many of the components of trauma and mental health-informed schools model three (detailed below) as possible. This model is supported by evidence-based research which shows positive change in well-being and mental health, when implemented successfully and consistently.
Encourage an appetite for life.
Develop brain capacities for emotional regulation.
Develop a capacity for empathy.
Model three: Protect, relate, regulate and reflect
Protect – Our priority with any child in school, is to ensure safety first. It is the foundation on which everything else depends. Our focus is not only on the physical environment, but also on the relational environment and the very culture and ethos of our school. We aim to never place a child in a situation that they are not able to manage. We do this through:
Relate – We agree the ability to form meaningful relationships is fundamental to mental health and happiness. It is the quality of contact we have with other people that is arguably the most important factor in our quality of life. Therefore we see the importance in:
Regulate – We recognise that a high ACE score without the support of emotionally available adults, is likely to damage the children’s minds, brains and bodies. This is due to a high level of toxic stress, therefore we place great emphasis on supporting children in such a way that means we don’t leave them in a state of toxic stress. We do this by:
Reflect – It is important when supporting a child’s emotional and mental health to have those conversations around ‘big’ and difficult feelings. We reject the notion that “this is opening a can of worms”. “If I can’t reflect on my feelings, I am far more likely to behave my feelings”. We need to support them to understand their thoughts and feelings, body sensations and reactions and encourage them to identify new options and strategies for ways forward, with both their hopes and difficulties. We can do this by:
We feel that our ‘way of being’ and all of our SEMH interventions listed below support all of the three TIS models.
Whole school approach to SEMH.
Optimally active play and attachment systems.
Constantly celebrating the positives.
Non-shaming developmentally appropriate sanctions.
Repeated positive relational experiences with emotionally-available adults.
Supported regulation by emotionally-available adults.
Provision of regulation spaces and tools.
Teaching stress regulation.
Whole school training on dysregulation.
Helping children to heal emotionally.
Conveying empathy through naming their pain.
Interventions
We are committed to continually moving forward and implementing new interventions based on research. This is to ensure the relational and emotional health of all our children, and allow our most vulnerable to feel safe and emotionally healthy to successfully access the classroom or at the very least, the opportunity to develop into mentally and physically healthy adults.
CARE de-escalation scripts zones of regulations.
Learning Mentor/ PE mentor, job role ELSAs.

Reading and Phonics Scheme
To support our children’s development of their reading skills, the school has elected to teach phonics using Unlocking Letters & Sounds. The teaching team also draw upon a range of resources to meet the needs of our learners to ensure they can begin and further develop their skills to read words.
Skilled word-reading involves working out the pronunciation of unfamiliar printed words (decoding) and recognising familiar printed words. Underpinning both of these is the understanding that letters represent the sounds in spoken words. Fluent decoding supports pupils’ comprehension, because they do not have to devote mental energy to individual words. A good grasp of phonics is also important for spelling, contributing to fluency and confidence in writing. Unlocking Letters and Sounds sets out a detailed and systematic programme for teaching phonic skills for children with the aim of them becoming fluent readers by age seven. Unlocking Letters and sounds sessions take place in reception, year 1 and year 2.
The school has elected to support the teaching of reading using a range of books from well-known authors, both fiction and non-fiction, these books form our MPS Reading Spine. In addition, a range of text types from the DfE validated Oxford Reading Tree reading programme ensures pupils have access to appropriate levelled texts for home and class reading.

Your child’s progress
We offer a variety of opportunities to share information about your child’s progress with you. There are parents’ evenings in the autumn and spring terms and a detailed written report in the summer term. The class teachers are available at the end of the day and frequently have informal feedback sessions with parents about pupils progress. If we are concerned a child is not making anticipated progress, we will arrange to meet with parents to discuss how we can work together to improve rates of progress. In some cases we may work with the Learning Support Adviser or education psychologist.
Concerns
If you have any concerns about your child, their progress or their behaviour either in school or out of school, please come in and talk with us. Your child’s teacher will be available at the end of the day and you can either book an appointment directly with them or arrange this through our school reception. If your matter is urgent, please come into reception and an appointment with a senior member of staff will be arranged as soon as possible.
Supporting your child’s learning at home
As you know, your involvement in your child’s learning is crucial to help them grow into well-rounded young people. You can help your child by supporting them with their reading, spelling and times tables. Furthermore, when they go to secondary school, they will be expected to complete ‘homework tasks’ and organise themselves (to manage work) at home on their own. As a school, it is our duty to help them do this as they grow.
Below is a link to an overview of the learning at home we expect your children to complete. They will be rewarded for completing their learning on a weekly basis.
We understand how busy life is, so taking this short amount of time each week with your child is really important. It will help them in their learning, provide opportunities of quality time to spend with your child and support them to prepare for secondary school.

The Cabot Learning Federation is a family of 36 schools in Bristol, Gloucestershire, South Gloucestershire, North Somerset and Somerset. We are a mature multi-academy trust (MAT) serving communities in the South West. We lead the Five Counties Teaching School Hubs Alliance and School-Centred Initial Teacher Training (SCITT) and the Boolean Maths Hub, professional development provisions delivered from our CLF Institute.
​Instinctively collaborative and ambitious, our trust supports 18,000 children and young people aged 2 to 19 in a diverse array of settings and more than 3,000 employees. Whether you are a school or MAT wishing to join our family, an educator looking for a new opportunity or a parent or young person who simply wants to find out more about us, welcome and we look forward to hearing from you.

Curriculum overview
Our Curriculum
In building our curriculum we have considered the needs of our pupils and their families and the social context within which they live. We believe that in order to enable our pupils to learn effectively, they need to have their uniqueness recognised and valued, feel safe in their environment and have the oral, social and emotional literacy skills to support them with the demands of life. We stress the importance of supporting emotional wellbeing and promoting personal development, recognising that many of our pupils do not come to school ‘ready to learn’ but have an appetite to gain skills, knowledge and understanding.
Our curriculum therefore has a number of key strands:
To enable every pupil to achieve their personal best;
To inspire enthusiasm and curiosity for learning and a determination to succeed;
To promote a values-based approach so that pupils take responsibility for themselves academically, socially and emotionally, morally and physically;
To prepare pupils to become successful and resilient members of their community and lifelong learners.
Our curriculum is underpinned by the teaching of basic skills while providing a range of opportunities through visits, visitors and practical first-hand learning experiences. Our assemblies and PHSE lessons promote positive attitudes, building a sense of belonging and community.Community involvement is a key element enabling the pupils to be visibly contributing to the well-being of others through visits, music and joint learning with parents and carers.
Knowledge organisers are used to make learning memorable and support the learning gateway themes. They include the key vocabulary that we expect pupils to recall and use in their learning. We fundamentally believe that providing our children with a richer and more varied vocabulary along with core skills will help them to be confident and resilient in the future.
Our curriculum is built upon five key foundations:
Through research and quality professional development, our teachers are experts in the subjects that they are teaching. Their passion and depth of understanding will ensure that the children are enthused and inspired by their new found knowledge. Each year of teaching will build upon the prior learning set down.
‘Metacognition’ is the process of thinking about thinking. In all our learning, we provide children with the metacognitive tools (or ‘thinking’ tools) that they need to organise their understanding. By engaging with our curriculum, we will teach our children to become critical and resilient thinkers who are not only confident to ask questions, but who are informed and articulate enough to ask the right questions. Polished
Throughout the curriculum, children’s learning will work towards a purposeful final product. We believe that there is much learning in the process of evaluating and editing. Carefully considered feedback from adults enables children to make substantial progress when planning, developing, honing and producing a finished product.
Oracy and Vocabulary
A love of language and effective communication is central to our curriculum. We ensure that our children speak with enthusiasm from their earliest years and rapidly acquire the skills that they need to be confident, but considered and considerate orators.
Providing our children with memorable experiences is key to our curriculum offer. We ensure that every area of learning is supplemented with visits and trips, encounters and adventures which will equip them with the confidence, knowledge and skills they need for a successful, happy and productive life.
Rationale:
So that the pupils at Minerva Primary School feel completely immersed in their curriculum; achieve the highest standards; and embed new, essential knowledge, we must ensure that we have a curriculum that is designed to assess appropriately, pre-learn where appropriate and re-visit regularly (daily, weekly, termly, yearly). This curriculum design ensures that pupils get a rich curriculum where the essential knowledge is covered repeatedly, while taking steps of progress to deepen and widen their knowledge as they move through the school.

SEND
At Minerva Primary school, we believe all children are equally valued. Through our school’s ethos, mission statement, aims, policies, practices and provision, we strive to eliminate barriers to learning and to develop an environment where all children can flourish and feel safe. We are committed to giving all our children every opportunity to achieve the highest of standards.
We pay particular attention to the provision of work meeting needs for all learners and the ongoing identification and achievement of specific targets.
At Minerva Primary school, every teacher is a teacher of SEND. Therefore, inclusion is a thread which runs through every area of the school, enhanced by collaboration between senior leaders, teachers, support staff, external agencies, parents and most importantly, the child.
We believe all children are unique individuals and at Minerva Primary school they are equipped to make progress so they achieve their best and become confident individuals who know the positive contribution they have to make to the world.
The Special Educational Needs Co-ordinator (SENCo) at Minerva Primary School is Rachelle Billington. If you would like to speak to Mrs Billington with regards to your child’s learning, please make an appointment via the school office.
